title: First visit to the gurdwara
hookLine: a baby's first visit, often with karah prashad for all
tomorrow: Fateh's hair is one big tangle, and he wants it cut. now what?

lines: WHAT YOU DON'T HAVE TO DO.
cards: Rule books usually tell you what to do. Every so often one stops to say what you don't have to do, and that's where the interesting history hides. The Sikh code of conduct has one of those lines.

Once the mother is able to get up and bathe, the family goes to the gurdwara, and the code adds: no matter how many days it's been. Why would a rule book bother to say that? Simran found out the hard way.
After the naming, an older neighbor told Bhua Preet she'd brought Sehaj out far too soon.

teach.b: Here's the puzzle solved. Around the Gurus, a custom called sutak treated a house with a new birth as impure for a set time; the mother and the baby were kept apart. The neighbor was speaking from that world.
Guru Nanak answers it in Asa di Var, on ang 472. In paraphrase: if you believe in impurity, then it's everywhere, in the cow dung, in the firewood, in every grain. Real impurity is somewhere else.
The mind's impurity is greed. The tongue's is a lie. The eyes' is staring at what isn't yours.
And then, in paraphrase again: birth and death come by the Hukam, the Order. A birth isn't a stain to wait out. It's the Hukam at work.
So the code sets no count of days. The mother comes when her body is ready, and the baby comes with her. And what happens when they arrive?
Karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is shared out to everyone sitting there. Not only to the family. Strangers get the same handful.
A baby who can't eat a crumb yet is welcomed by feeding the whole room.
That's the first visit: not a quarantine ending, but a sangat getting one person bigger.

how: Sikh families bring a new baby to the gurdwara once the mother is able, with no fixed waiting period; hymns and Ardas are said, and karah prashad is shared with everyone in the sangat.

games.q: what does “first visit to the gurdwara” mean?
o: a baby's first time with the sangat, sweet shared with all
a home blessing held before the baby is born
the day a child first reads aloud from the Granth

games.q: the puzzle and its answer — tap the pairs.
p: a birth treated as impure for a time
shared with everyone in the room

s: the Sikh code asks a new mother to stay home for a set number of days
it says the family comes once she's able, no matter how many days it's been.
Guru Nanak says the impurity of the tongue is a lie
Asa di Var, ang 472: real impurity is greed, lies and envy, not a birth.
at a baby's first visit, the karah prashad is only for the family
it's shared out to everyone sitting in the sangat, strangers included.

games.q: a friend just had a baby and says her relatives want her indoors for weeks "to stay pure." she's Sikh and asks what the Gurus said. you say:
o: Guru Nanak called the impurity of birth an idea to drop; come when your body's ready.
the Gurus agreed, so it's safest to wait the full time first.
the Gurus said to bring the baby on the very next day.
games.why: on ang 472 Guru Nanak says birth comes by the Hukam and real impurity is greed and lies. the code sets no count of days, only the mother's readiness.

practice: Bring to mind someone new in your circle: a baby, a neighbor who just moved in, someone starting at your work or school. Send them a short welcome, plain and warm.
Then sit with your phone face down and let the welcome be the last thing you did.

wordCard.voice: First visit to the gurdwara. A baby's first time with the sangat, whenever the mother is ready, with karah prashad for the whole room.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sutak, the impurity some believed a birth brought. Guru Nanak's salok turns it toward the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: the first visit. No waiting it out, just a room that grows by one. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, the chapter on birth and naming ceremonies (the family comes once the mother is able, irrespective of the number of days)
Ang 472 (Asa di Var, saloks of Guru Nanak on sootak: jae kar sootak manneeai; man kaa sootak lobh hai; jaman marnaa hukam hai), paraphrased
